<!-- Sensitivity checks of the migrant report, knitted in as a child document when show_sensitivity is TRUE in its config chunk; it uses the report's objects and does not render on its own -->

## Supplementary sensitivity checks {#sec-sensitivity}

**Season term.** These comparisons use the 15 October season of the single-species models, including the earlier multi-species base model on that season. With period intercepts, a linear day of season varied within periods almost only between October-December 2016 and March 2017, both forest only, so its slope was one forest contrast extended across the whole season; it predicted occupancy rising steadily from October to March, which is not plausible for wintering birds. I therefore replaced it with the arrival-period indicator. Its end, `r arrival_end_date`, follows eBird Status and Trends, which shows *S. striata*'s non-breeding distribution settled in South America by late November to early December; *S. striata* arrives later than most other migrants, so the date is conservative for the community. The indicator is estimated from the 2016-17 forest data (all November 2019 location-periods fall before `r arrival_end_date`, so in 2019 it is absorbed by that period's intercept). In the single-species models, use was lower during arrival for *S. striata* (`r est(arrival_ss$Setophaga_striata)`), less clearly for *S. ruticilla* (`r est(arrival_ss$Setophaga_ruticilla)`), and not for *P. rubra* (`r est(arrival_ss$Piranga_rubra)`). The choice of season term left every habitat contrast unchanged; WAIC with a linear day of season, no season term and the arrival indicator was `r paste(map_chr(names(season_waic), \(k) paste0(if (k == "Community") "multi-species model" else paste0("*", species_label(k), "*"), " ", paste(sprintf("%.1f", season_waic[[k]]), collapse = " / "))), collapse = "; ")` (the multi-species arrival fit with doubled chains). An arrival period ending 1 November, where per-visit detection of any migrant in forest jumped in our data, could not be estimated: *S. striata*, *S. ruticilla* and *Mniotilta varia* were never detected before it, so their arrival coefficients drifted to extreme values (e.g. *S. striata* `r sprintf("%.1f", arrnov_sp[["Setophaga_striata"]])`) and the among-species variance of the arrival coefficient did not converge (Rhat `r sprintf("%.2f", arrnov_rhat)`). The checks below were fit before the arrival indicator and canopy cover were added, so they include a linear day of season and no canopy.

**Passage period (multi-species model).** Starting the multi-species season on `r comm_season_start_date` adds GAICA's 2019 distance-gradient surveys, which hold most passage detections of *C. virens* and *C. ustulatus* but none of `r paste0("*", species_label(names(passage_detections)[passage_detections == 0]), "*", collapse = ", ")`. In spOccupancy's multi-species models the missing values in the detection data must be the same for every species, so the window cannot differ by species; instead, the early location-periods are flagged as passage. On shorter chains (`r format(n_iter_short, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` iterations), I compared passage with arrival ending `r arrival_end_date`, passage with arrival ending `r comm_arrival_end_date`, and arrival ending `r arrival_end_date` alone: WAIC `r paste(sprintf("%.1f", sep24_waic), collapse = " / ")`. With arrival ending `r arrival_end_date`, the among-species variance of the passage coefficient did not converge (Rhat `r sprintf("%.2f", passage_rhat[["pass_dec1"]])`), as the species never detected during passage pushed their passage coefficients to extreme values; with arrival ending `r comm_arrival_end_date` it did (Rhat `r sprintf("%.2f", passage_rhat[["pass_nov15"]])`), and WAIC was lowest, so the base model uses that coding with doubled chains. The passage location-periods are exactly the distance-gradient locations, surveyed only by teams 1 and 2, so lower use during passage and lower detection by those teams are separated only by the repeat visits within location-periods.

**Rainfall.** Annual rainfall enters additively in the base models: it varies only between farms (`r farms_by_habitat[["Ssp"]]` silvopasture farms), and its interaction with habitat reversed sign when annual rainfall was replaced by driest-month rainfall.

**Reference level and prior.** Only `r det_lp_by_habitat$Setophaga_striata[["Pastizales"]]` of `r lp_by_habitat[["Pastizales"]]` pasture location-periods had an *S. striata* detection, so pasture occupancy is weakly identified and partly set by the prior. Refitting *S. striata* with pasture instead of forest as the reference level, which changes only which coefficients the priors act on, gave a silvopasture vs pasture contrast of `r est(striata_pref[, "HabitatSsp"])` instead of `r est(striata_nc_contrasts[["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])` (both without canopy cover); the earlier fit with separate 2016-17 periods and a quadratic in day of season gave `r est(striata_old[, "HabitatSsp"])`, so the reference level, not the period or season terms, moves it. The direction is robust, and silvopasture vs forest barely changed (`r est(contrasts_of(striata_pref)[["Silvopasture vs forest"]])` with pasture as reference).

Varying the prior directly gives the same picture. With the variance of the normal prior on the coefficients set to `r prior_vars[1]` and `r prior_vars[2]` instead of the default 2.72, *S. striata*'s silvopasture vs pasture contrast was `r est(striata_prior[["1"]][["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])` and `r est(striata_prior[["10"]][["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])` (default `r est(striata_nc_contrasts[["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])`; all three fits without canopy cover), and silvopasture vs forest `r est(striata_prior[["1"]][["Silvopasture vs forest"]])` and `r est(striata_prior[["10"]][["Silvopasture vs forest"]])`. In the multi-species model, with the same variances on the prior for the community-level means, the community-level mean silvopasture vs pasture contrast was `r est(comm_prior[["10"]][["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])` at variance `r prior_vars[2]`; at variance `r prior_vars[1]` the among-species variance of the silvopasture coefficient did not converge (Rhat `r sprintf("%.2f", rhat_ssp_var[["1"]])`), so that fit is not interpreted. The direction of every silvopasture contrast is robust to the prior; the size of silvopasture vs pasture is not.

**Why the first multi-species fit inflated the contrasts.** An earlier fit with pasture as the reference level gave larger contrasts against pasture than the single-species models (e.g. *S. striata* silvopasture vs pasture `r est(sp_draws(ms_old, "HabitatSsp", "Setophaga_striata"))` against `r est(striata_old[, "HabitatSsp"])` single-species). Its silvopasture and forest occupancy matched the single-species fits, but each species' pasture occupancy, then the intercept, was pulled toward a low community intercept set by the six rare species, which were detected almost only in forest. With forest, the best-sampled habitat, as the reference, the contrasts of the single- and multi-species models agree, and pasture occupancy under the prediction conditions is low in both models, with no consistent shift between them (*S. striata* `r occ_med(pasture_occ$Setophaga_striata$ss)` single-species vs `r occ_med(pasture_occ$Setophaga_striata$ms)` multi-species; *S. ruticilla* `r occ_med(pasture_occ$Setophaga_ruticilla$ss)` vs `r occ_med(pasture_occ$Setophaga_ruticilla$ms)`; *P. rubra* `r occ_med(pasture_occ$Piranga_rubra$ss)` vs `r occ_med(pasture_occ$Piranga_rubra$ms)`). The earlier fit also did not converge, because March 2017 surveyed only forest and its period intercept was not identified for species never detected then; merging the two 2016-17 periods fixed this in the base model (without canopy, the largest community-level Rhat left, `r sprintf("%.2f", rhat_comm(ms_fit_nc))`, is for the among-species variance of one team's warm-up slope in detection).

**Silvopasture's own slope with distance from the forest edge.** In the models above, pasture and silvopasture share one slope with distance outside forest. Letting silvopasture differ from pasture, the community-mean difference was `r est(comm_draws(ms_dist, "Ssp_Dist_open"))`, and all three well-detected species had flatter slopes in silvopasture than in pasture, though none clearly (*S. striata* `r est(sp_draws(ms_dist, "Ssp_Dist_open", "Setophaga_striata"))`, *S. ruticilla* `r est(sp_draws(ms_dist, "Ssp_Dist_open", "Setophaga_ruticilla"))`, *P. rubra* `r est(sp_draws(ms_dist, "Ssp_Dist_open", "Piranga_rubra"))`). WAIC did not change (`r sprintf("%.1f", waic[["dist"]])` vs `r sprintf("%.1f", waic[["base"]])`), and the largest community-level Rhat was `r sprintf("%.2f", rhat_comm(ms_dist))`, for the among-species variance of the 2016-17 period intercept rather than the slope terms.

**Live fences vs dispersed trees.** Splitting silvopasture into live fences (`r sum(ss_l$occ.covs$Habitat_split == "Live_fence")` locations within the season window) and dispersed trees (`r sum(ss_l$occ.covs$Habitat_split == "Dispersed_trees")`) asks more than the migrant data can answer: the among-species variance of the dispersed-trees effect did not converge (Rhat `r sprintf("%.2f", ms_split$rhat$tau.sq.beta[colnames(ms_split$tau.sq.beta.samples) == "Habitat_splitDispersed_trees"])`), and WAIC did not change (`r sprintf("%.1f", waic[["split"]])`). *S. striata* tended to use dispersed trees more than live fences (live fence minus dispersed trees `r est(lf_minus_dt(ms_split, "Setophaga_striata"))`), which fits its higher use with more silvopasture cover nearby, since dispersed-tree points have more silvopasture cover within 300 m than live-fence points (mean `r ssp_by_sub[["Dispersed_trees"]]`% vs `r ssp_by_sub[["Live_fence"]]`% over surveyed location-periods). The split is better tested in the 98-species model.

**Canopy cover and the spatial random effect.** In the multi-species model, the shared spatial factor's effective range shortened from `r sprintf("%.1f", ring_row("Community", NA, "full")$Range_km)` km without canopy to `r sprintf("%.1f", ring_row("Community", comm_radius, "full")$Range_km)` km when including canopy cover `r ring_km(comm_radius)`. This suggests that canopy explains part of the spatial pattern the spatial random effect carried without it. Without the spatial random effect (a location random effect in its place), the `r ring_km(comm_radius)` ring still improved WAIC (ΔWAIC `r sprintf("%.1f", nonsp_dwaic)` against the same model without canopy), and the canopy coefficients barely changed: community-level mean `r est(nonsp_comm)`, *S. striata* `r est(nonsp_sp$Setophaga_striata)`, *C. ustulatus* `r est(nonsp_sp$Catharus_ustulatus)` per 10 percentage points. The canopy effect therefore does not depend on the spatial random effect it partly replaces.
